moves.spoken: You played perfectly — for the home stretch, let's go. e4, c5.
This is a Sicilian — the knight to f3.
The line I told you to play here is to push d4 next — you want to open it up; it's literally called the Open Sicilian.
c-takes-d4, the knight recaptures on d4.
Now you don't want to react to this — if he takes your knight, you can simply recapture with the queen, so you can just develop normally.
The knight to c3. Now, your bishops — where do they belong?
f4 for one bishop — but you mean the light-squared bishop.
The dark-squared bishop is more active than f4 — and f4 blunders a fork to e5 — so you can put it on g5.
If he goes e5 — think about his knight on f6; he's actually weakened himself.
If you take the knight on f6, notice that he has to ruin his entire pawn structure by recapturing with the pawn — so I would.
Now I would immediately prepare to castle queenside, because you're going to attack him on the kingside, and you want to tuck your king away.
Your queen is defending the knight, so you want to keep it on the d-file — I'd put it on d2, and prevent Black's ideas.
Now he's attacking your knight — how can you defend it?
Where can you put it? The knight to b3 would be good, because it stops him from taking the pawn on b2 — a low-key move, but a good one.
And look at his queen on b6 — you can attack that queen in the future, but complete your development first.
So now I'm castling queenside, and then to attack the queen it's bringing the knight over to a4.
So he takes this first —
do you take back with the c-pawn? Yes, the c-pawn is good, keeping the a-pawn where it closes up the a-file.
Whoa — he takes on b3?
That came out of nowhere — a-takes-b3.
The confidence with which that was played! The knight to b4.
But let's not relax — you have some developing to do. The bishop to b5 with check.
Now you have a fork — let's practice that thing I tortured you with previously: what are the undefended pieces and pawns, and how can you attack two of them at once?
The undefended pawns: d6 is defended by the bishop, but f6 is completely undefended, and the knight is ready — forks. The queen to d4.
That was really the mistake he made — but careful, there's a trap hiding under the surface.

Now you can take the pawn — the queen takes f6 with check — but if he moves his king out, you actually can't take the rook, and that's the entire point of his variation. What if he covers with the bishop?

The king to c7. So you can't take the rook, because of a check on h6 — so do the next best thing, take the stuff that you can take. He'll probably go the king to b6, and then you have a sexy move: a check on a4 with the knight — and I want you to tell me why we're not blundering the bishop. He might think you blundered it. Then it's checkmate — c4, even sexier than the mate I had in mind, because you dropped the piece back; the knight from the rim is defending b6.
The queen takes b3 made it a little bit easier for you, but everything was pretty straightforward. What do you say we do one last one for the road?

Was that queen play an accident, or did he get anything out of it? Zero — he gives up a queen for a pawn; I think it might have been a mis-click, one of those pre-move accidents, but other than that I honestly have no idea what went through his mind. Okay, in this next game — e3, the c-file is opening; maybe he'll play e4 and transpose. This is like a reverse French, and in a position like this, a lot of times what I do is just push e4, closing up the centre — a different type of position, and one of the next steps to improvement.
